title: Part III: Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era

learn.hook: India's Constitution was not written in a day. It was argued over, clause by clause, for nearly three years by an Assembly representing a vast and divided country.
points: The Constitution of India came into effect on 26 January 1950. It is among the longest constitutions in the world, reflecting the country's size and diversity.

It was framed between December 1946 and November 1949. Drafts were discussed clause by clause in the Constituent Assembly over eleven sessions, with sittings spread over 165 days; between sessions, committees and sub-committees revised the drafts.
The Constituent Assembly Debates (CAD), the printed record of these discussions, run into eleven bulky volumes and are a major source for historians.

The Constitution was framed against a backdrop of deep diversity and division: a country of many religions, languages, castes and regions, recovering from colonial rule and torn by the violence of Partition. It had to bind together a diverse people and set out a democratic future.

Timeline: 26 July 1945 Labour government in Britain; December 1945–January 1946 general elections in India; 16 May 1946 Cabinet Mission announces its scheme; 16 August 1946 Direct Action Day; 9 December 1946 Constituent Assembly begins; 13 December 1946 Objectives Resolution; 15 August 1947 independence and partition; 26 November 1949 Constitution adopted; 26 January 1950 Constitution comes into effect.

learn.hook: The years before the Constitution saw a navy mutiny, a national army formed abroad, horrific riots and the partition of the country. The framers wrote with these fresh in their minds.
points: The years before the Constitution were tumultuous. The Quit India Movement of 1942 was the last mass movement against British rule. Subhas Chandra Bose had formed the Indian National Army (INA) to fight the British with armed struggle.

In the spring of 1946, ratings of the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) mutinied in Bombay and other cities, in sympathy with the INA and against British rule. There were strikes and protests by workers and peasants across the country.

There was also bitter communal conflict: the Great Calcutta Killings of August 1946 were followed by riots across north and east India, and then by the violence of Partition in 1947, which uprooted millions and killed hundreds of thousands.

Another major problem was the integration of the princely states. During the Raj, roughly one-third of the subcontinent's area was ruled by Nawabs and Maharajas who owed allegiance to the British Crown. At independence their status was uncertain, and some rulers dreamt of independence.
These experiences of violence and fragmentation shaped the framers' concerns: unity, stability, a strong centre and protection for all citizens.

example.q: How did the tumultuous events of 1946–47 shape the concerns of the framers?

So the framers stressed unity, a strong centre and rights for all.
example.answer: They made the framers concerned with national unity, stability and protecting the rights of all citizens.

topics.title: The making of the Constituent Assembly

learn.hook: The Constituent Assembly was not elected by every adult Indian. Its members were chosen by provincial legislatures elected on a limited franchise.
points: The members of the Constituent Assembly were not elected on the basis of universal adult franchise. In the winter of 1945–46 provincial elections were held, and the provincial legislatures then chose the representatives to the Constituent Assembly, following the Cabinet Mission plan.

The Muslim League chose to boycott the Constituent Assembly, preferring to press its demand for Pakistan with a separate constitution. The Socialists too were initially unwilling to join, believing the Assembly was a creation of the British.
As a result, the Congress dominated the Assembly: about 82 per cent of its members were also members of the Congress.

But Congress members did not speak in one voice. They differed on critical issues: some were inspired by socialism, others defended landlordism; some were close to communal parties, others were assertively secular. Discussions were therefore lively and real.
The Constituent Assembly had 300 members. Many debates were influenced by public opinion, as arguments in the Assembly were reported in newspapers and discussed widely.

example.q: Was the Constituent Assembly representative of all Indians? Give reasons.
steps: Its members were indirectly elected by provincial legislatures, not by universal franchise.

example.answer: Not fully, since it was indirectly elected and some groups stayed away, but diverse opinions within it and public debate made it more representative than its composition suggests.

topics.title: The dominant voices and public opinion

learn.hook: Six members played particularly important roles, but the Constitution was also shaped by a constitutional advisor, a chief draughtsman, and thousands of ordinary citizens who wrote in!
points: Six members of the Constituent Assembly played especially important roles. Three were Congress leaders: Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Rajendra Prasad.

Nehru moved the crucial Objectives Resolution and the resolution proposing the National Flag as a 'horizontal tricolour of saffron, white and dark green in equal proportion', with a wheel in navy blue at the centre. Patel worked mostly behind the scenes, helping draft reports and reconciling opposing points of view. Rajendra Prasad was the President of the Assembly, steering discussions along constructive lines and making sure all members had a chance to speak.

B.R. Ambedkar, the lawyer and economist, served as Chairman of the Drafting Committee and guided the Draft Constitution through the Assembly. Two other lawyers, K.M. Munshi from Gujarat and Alladi Krishnaswamy Aiyar from Madras, gave crucial inputs.

Two civil servants were important too: B.N. Rau, Constitutional Advisor to the Government of India, who prepared background papers on constitutions of other countries; and S.N. Mukherjee, the chief draughtsman, who could put complex proposals into clear legal language.

Public opinion also mattered. Arguments in the Assembly were reported in newspapers, and proposals were publicly debated. The Assembly invited suggestions from the public, and hundreds of responses were received, from linguistic groups, caste associations, religious organisations and others.

learn.hook: On 13 December 1946, Nehru stood up and moved a resolution that defined what free India would be: an independent sovereign republic guaranteeing justice, liberty and equality.
points: On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru introduced the 'Objectives Resolution' in the Constituent Assembly. It was a momentous resolution that outlined the defining ideals of the Constitution and provided the framework within which constitution-making was to proceed.

It proclaimed India to be an 'Independent Sovereign Republic', guaranteed its citizens justice, equality and freedom, and assured that 'adequate safeguards shall be provided for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and Depressed and Other Backward Classes'.

Nehru placed the Indian effort in a long historical tradition of struggles for liberty. He referred to the American and French Revolutions and the making of their constitutions, and to the Soviet Revolution and its emphasis on economic justice.

He stressed that the Indian Constitution would not merely copy others. The objective was to blend liberal ideas of democracy with the socialist idea of economic justice and re-adapt them within the Indian context.
The ideals of the Objectives Resolution later found expression in the Preamble of the Constitution.

topics.title: The will of the people and Somnath Lahiri's critique

learn.hook: A Communist member, Somnath Lahiri, warned that the 'dark hand of British imperialism' still hung over the Assembly. Was the Assembly truly free?
points: Nehru argued that the Constitution would be an expression of the will of the people. The Constituent Assembly was expected to express the aspirations of those who had participated in the movement for independence.
Democracy, equality and justice were ideals that had become intimately associated with social struggles in India since the nineteenth century. The Constitution was meant to embody these aspirations.
Not everyone was convinced. Somnath Lahiri, a Communist member, saw the dark hand of British imperialism hanging over the deliberations of the Assembly.

He pointed out that the Constituent Assembly was British-made: it was working according to the Cabinet Mission plan, and British officials could still influence the outcome. He urged members, and Indians in general, to free themselves fully from the influences of imperial rule.

Lahiri's critique reminds historians that the Assembly met before full independence, under conditions set by the departing colonial power, and that members held very different views about its legitimacy.

topics.title: Defining rights: the debate on separate electorates

learn.hook: In August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur pleaded for separate electorates for Muslims. Many argued fiercely against it, and by 1949 even some Muslim members had changed their minds.
points: How were the rights of individual citizens and of minority groups to be defined? One fiercely debated question was whether separate electorates should continue.

On 27 August 1947, B. Pocker Bahadur from Madras made a powerful plea for continuing separate electorates. He argued that minorities exist in all lands and cannot be wished away; a political system was needed in which minorities could live in harmony with others and have a meaningful say in governance. Separate electorates, he felt, would ensure Muslims a voice.

Most nationalist leaders opposed this. They argued that separate electorates had divided people, been used by the British to divide and rule, and led to Partition. Sardar Patel called separate electorates a 'poison' that had entered the body politic.

G.B. Pant argued that separate electorates were not only harmful for the nation but also for the minorities, as they would permanently isolate minorities and make them vulnerable. He believed citizens should be loyal to the state and not to their community.

By 1949, most Muslim members of the Assembly agreed that separate electorates were against the interests of the minorities. Begum Aizaz Rasul felt they were self-destructive because they isolated minorities from the majority; Muslims should instead take an active part in the democratic process.

learn.hook: N.G. Ranga said the real minorities were the poor. Jaipal Singh, captain of India's 1928 Olympic gold-winning hockey team, spoke for India's tribes. Both asked for more than words.
points: N.G. Ranga, a socialist who had been a leader of the peasant movement, welcomed the Objectives Resolution but urged that the term 'minorities' be interpreted in economic terms. For him, the real minorities were the poor and the downtrodden.

Ranga argued that legal rights alone would mean nothing to the poor unless they were provided the conditions to make use of them. He said, 'We will need much more than this Resolution'. Ordinary people, including the adivasis, needed protection and support to escape poverty and exploitation.

Jaipal Singh, a tribal leader who had captained India's hockey team at the 1928 Olympics, spoke eloquently on behalf of the tribes. He said tribes were not a numerical minority, but they needed protection.

He explained that tribal people had been dispossessed of the land they had settled, deprived of their forests and pastures, and forced to move. They were looked down upon as primitive and backward by others.

Jaipal Singh pleaded for measures to protect the tribes and to break the physical and emotional distance between tribal and non-tribal society, including reservation of seats in the legislature, so that tribals could have their voices heard.

topics.title: 'We were suppressed for thousands of years': the depressed castes

learn.hook: J. Nagappa told the Assembly: 'We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more.' The Constitution responded by abolishing untouchability.
points: Members from the depressed castes stressed that their problems could not be solved through protection and safeguards alone. Their disabilities were caused by the social norms and moral values of caste society, which had used their services and labour while keeping them at a social distance.

J. Nagappa from Madras declared, 'We have been suffering, but we are prepared to suffer no more', and pointed out that the depressed castes were not numerically a minority (20 to 25 per cent of the population). K.J. Khanderkar of the Central Provinces said they had been 'suppressed for thousands of years'. Dakshayani Velayudhan, also from Madras, argued that what was needed was not all kinds of safeguards but the immediate removal of social disabilities.
During the national movement, B.R. Ambedkar had demanded separate electorates for the depressed castes, which Gandhi opposed. In the Constituent Assembly, the solution adopted was different.
It was recommended that untouchability be abolished, Hindu temples be thrown open to all castes, and seats in legislatures and jobs in government offices be reserved for the lowest castes.

Many recognised that not all problems could be solved through law; social attitudes had to change. But the Constitution guaranteed fundamental rights to all, abolished untouchability, and provided reservations as a democratic step towards equality.

topics.title: The powers of the state: three lists and K. Santhanam

learn.hook: K. Santhanam warned that if the provinces did not get enough money, they would soon be bankrupt. The debate on Centre versus states began on day one!
points: One of the most intensely debated topics was the respective rights of the Central government and the states.

The Draft Constitution provided three lists of subjects: Union, State and Concurrent. Subjects in the Union List were exclusively for the Centre, those in the State List for the states, and those in the Concurrent List were shared by both.

Many more items were placed under exclusive Union control than in other federations, and the Concurrent List was also longer than desired by the provinces. The Union also had control of minerals and key industries.

K. Santhanam from Madras argued that not only the states but also the Centre needed to be strengthened, and that an over-burdened Centre would not function effectively. He argued that the states needed adequate financial resources to carry out their responsibilities.

Santhanam warned that the proposed allocation of revenues would impoverish the provinces, which would soon be bankrupt and unable to undertake development; he predicted that if this was not addressed, the provinces might even rise in revolt against the Centre. Many members from the provinces echoed his fears.

topics.title: The case for a strong centre

learn.hook: Ambedkar declared he wanted 'a strong and united Centre, much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935'. Why?
points: Many members argued for a strong Centre. The violence of Partition and the fear of further fragmentation strengthened this case.
B.R. Ambedkar declared that he wanted 'a strong and united Centre, much stronger than the Centre we had created under the Government of India Act of 1935'.

Jawaharlal Nehru argued that now that Partition was a settled fact, a weak central authority would be injurious to the interests of the country, as it would be incapable of ensuring peace, coordinating vital matters of common concern and speaking effectively for the whole country internationally.

The Constitution gave the Centre significant powers: the Union List was long; Article 356 gave the Centre the power to take over a state's administration on the recommendation of the Governor; emergency provisions strengthened the Centre; and the Governor was appointed by the Centre.

Revenues were distributed so that some taxes (such as customs duties and company taxes) were held by the Centre, others (such as income tax and excise duties) were shared with the states, and some were assigned to the states. The result was a federal structure with a strong unitary bias.

topics.title: The language of the nation: Hindustani, Hindi and a compromise

learn.hook: R.V. Dhulekar told the Assembly that those who did not know Hindustani were not worthy to be members and had better leave! The House erupted.
points: By the 1930s the Congress had accepted that Hindustani should be the national language. Mahatma Gandhi felt that everyone should speak in a language that common people could easily understand.

Hindustani, a blend of Hindi and Urdu, was a popular language of a large section of people in north India, enriched by the interaction of diverse cultures. Over time, however, as communal conflicts deepened, Hindi and Urdu were drawn apart, with Hindi becoming more Sanskritised and Urdu more Persianised. Gandhi retained his faith in Hindustani.

R.V. Dhulekar, a Congressman from the United Provinces, made an aggressive plea that Hindi be used as the language of constitution-making. When told that not everyone knew the language, he said that those who did not know Hindustani were not worthy to be members of the Assembly and had better leave. This caused an uproar.
The Language Committee of the Assembly produced a compromise formula. Hindi in the Devanagari script would be the official language, but the transition to Hindi would be gradual.

For the first fifteen years, English would continue to be used for all official purposes. Each province was allowed to choose one of the regional languages for official work within the province. The term 'national language' was replaced by 'official language' to avoid controversy.

topics.title: The fear of domination and a Constitution of compromise

learn.hook: G. Durgabai had worked to spread Hindustani in the south at Gandhi's call. Yet she warned the Assembly that pushing Hindi aggressively would create fear and opposition.
points: Shrimati G. Durgabai from Madras explained her worries about how the language discussion was developing. She said opposition to Hindi in the south was very strong; people felt it was a fight for their existence. She herself had accepted Gandhi's call to propagate Hindustani in the south, but felt that the aggressive push for Hindi had created fear.

T.A. Ramalingam Chettiar from Madras emphasised that whatever was done had to be done with caution. The cause of Hindi would not be served if it was pushed too aggressively. The fears of people, even if unjustified, had to be allayed, or there would be bitter feelings. There should be give and take, and no question of imposition.
The final arrangement allowed regional languages to be used for official work within provinces, and English continued for a transitional period, so that no group felt dominated.

The language debate, like those on rights and federalism, shows that the Constitution was a product of intense debate, disagreement and compromise. Members listened to opposing views, changed their minds, and found solutions acceptable to most.

The Constitution addressed both the past and the present: it responded to the legacy of colonial rule, caste discrimination and separate electorates, and to the present crisis of Partition violence and diversity, by guaranteeing rights, creating a strong Centre and protecting linguistic and cultural diversity.

The compromise: Hindi as official language with a gradual transition, English for fifteen years, regional languages in provinces.
example.answer: It was divisive because of fears of domination; it was resolved through compromise that respected linguistic diversity.
